A SOC or security analyst cares because insufficient logging and monitoring is itself a recognized vulnerability that lets attacks go undetected, and analysts must ensure critical events are captured and forwarded to a SIEM for correlation and alerting.
logging and monitoring.exam: The exam may test how cloud service models (IaaS, PaaS, SaaS) affect logging visibility and why insufficient logging and monitoring is treated as a vulnerability that delays detection.

explain: A platform in this context is the software architecture that defines what functions an application performs and where each of those functions actually executes.

Architecture is analyzed by decomposing an application into layers such as presentation logic (the user interface), business logic (processing and rules), storage (data persistence), and the communication that links them, then mapping which tier or system each layer runs on.
Understanding this distribution reveals where sensitive processing and data live and therefore where trust boundaries and attack surfaces exist.

A security analyst cares because knowing what happens and where it happens is a prerequisite for threat modeling, choosing the right security controls per tier, and assessing how a vulnerability in one layer can affect the whole system.
platforms.exam: On the exam you may need to identify the architectural layer (presentation, business logic, storage, or communication) relevant to a described weakness or control placement.

explain: Common application architecture types describe how processing and data are distributed across systems, ranging from fully centralized to fully distributed designs.

Host-based architecture runs everything on a single central system with dumb terminals; client-based runs the application on the endpoint; client/server splits work between an endpoint client and a central server; and distributed or n-tier architecture spreads presentation, application, and data functions across multiple separate layers or servers.
Each model shifts the trust boundaries and attack surface, so a monolithic host concentrates risk on one system while an n-tier design multiplies the network communication paths that must be secured.

A security analyst cares because identifying the architecture type determines where controls belong, how components communicate, and which tiers hold the sensitive data and logic an attacker would target.
common architecture types.exam: CS0-003 may ask you to match an architecture type such as client/server or n-tier to its security implications or to where a control should be applied.

explain: Software considerations are the deployment models an application can use, each carrying distinct security trade-offs that shape how it should be assessed and protected.

A thick (or fat) client performs substantial processing locally in a client/server model, a thin client relies on a central server with minimal local logic, a web application is a distributed browser-based design, mobile apps run on portable devices, and embedded software is self-contained code running on dedicated hardware, with a system-on-chip (SoC) being an especially compact embedded form.

Where code and data execute changes the attack surface, so a thick client exposes logic on the endpoint for reverse engineering while a web application concentrates risk in server-side and browser-facing components.

A security analyst cares because the software type dictates the appropriate testing approach, patching strategy, and controls, since embedded and mobile software in particular are often harder to update and monitor than server-based applications.
software considerations.exam: Expect questions distinguishing thick versus thin clients, web, mobile, and embedded/SoC software and matching each to its characteristic vulnerabilities or update challenges.

explain: Service-Oriented Architecture (SOA) is a design in which clients consume discrete, reusable services through APIs, typically over web protocols, using a loosely coupled connection so services can change independently of the clients that call them.

SOA connections may be persistent (a maintained session) or non-persistent (per-request), and the architecture can be open (exposed to external consumers) or closed (internal only), while cloud computing makes SOA far easier to scale on demand.

Because services are loosely coupled and exposed via APIs, SOA relies on standards like Security Assertions Markup Language (SAML) to carry authentication and authorization assertions between the identity provider and the services a client consumes.

A security analyst cares because each exposed service is an attack surface requiring its own authentication, authorization, and input validation, and misconfigured federation or API security in a SOA can allow unauthorized cross-service access.
service-oriented architecture (soa).exam: The exam may reference SAML as the standard for SOA authentication and authorization or test the security implications of loosely coupled, API-consumed services.

explain: DevOps is a culture and set of practices that integrate software development with IT operations so the two functions collaborate continuously rather than working in separate silos.

It gives operations direct input into software functionality and quality while giving developers timely, real-world feedback on how their code behaves in production, typically supported by automation, continuous integration, and continuous delivery pipelines.
This tighter loop accelerates release cadence and improves reliability, but the automation and shared pipelines it introduces also create new assets that must be secured.
A security analyst cares because faster, automated releases can propagate vulnerabilities to production just as quickly, making pipeline security and early testing essential.
devops.exam: On the exam DevOps is contrasted with DevSecOps, where you must recognize that DevOps alone does not inherently build security into the pipeline.

explain: DevSecOps extends DevOps by integrating security as a shared responsibility throughout the entire development and operations lifecycle rather than treating it as a final gate.
By embedding automated security testing, code analysis, and controls into the CI/CD pipeline, it raises the priority of security so it is designed in from the start instead of bolted on afterward.
This shift-left approach is more effective and far cheaper because flaws found and fixed during design and coding cost far less to remediate than those discovered in production.

A security analyst cares because DevSecOps operationalizes continuous vulnerability management, giving the SOC earlier visibility into weaknesses and reducing the volume of defects that ever reach a live environment.
devsecops.exam: CS0-003 emphasizes DevSecOps as building security in early (shift-left) and integrating automated security testing into the pipeline rather than adding security later.

explain: Coding requirements are the specifications that define how software must behave, and they are grouped into functional, non-functional, and security categories that together drive secure development.

Functional requirements describe the inputs, processes, and outputs the software must produce; non-functional requirements define characteristics such as acceptable character inputs, input constraints, performance, and system limitations; and security requirements specify the behaviors and characteristics needed to meet defined security levels, including how the system safely interacts with other systems.
Capturing these requirements up front lets developers build validation, constraints, and protective behaviors directly into the code rather than discovering gaps after deployment.

A security analyst cares because vague or missing security and input requirements are a root cause of injection, overflow, and logic flaws, so reviewing requirements is an early and cost-effective point to prevent vulnerabilities.
coding requirements.exam: Expect the exam to distinguish functional, non-functional, and security requirements and to stress defining input constraints and security behaviors early to prevent vulnerabilities.

explain: Many of the most damaging attacks (SQL injection, command injection, buffer overflows, and cross-site scripting) succeed because an application accepts data from a user and then treats that data as trusted, so the single most effective defense is rigorous input validation on every field the application receives.

The strongest validation strategy is allow-listing (also called positive validation): define exactly what valid input looks like in terms of type, length, format, and range, process only input that matches, and outright reject anything that does not rather than trying to sanitize or 'cleanse' malicious content.
Attempting to strip or escape bad characters is fragile because attackers constantly find new encodings and bypasses, whereas rejecting non-conforming input closes the gap entirely.

A SOC analyst cares because the majority of web and application compromises they investigate trace back to missing or weak input validation, and knowing this shapes both remediation recommendations and detection rules.
attack types.exam: Expect scenario questions asking for the best mitigation against injection or XSS, where the correct answer is input validation using an allow-list rather than blocklist filtering or output-only sanitization.

explain: Privilege escalation is when an attacker who already has some level of access attempts to gain rights beyond what they are authorized to hold, ideally reaching an administrator or root account that controls the whole system.

Vertical escalation moves from a lower-privileged account to a higher one (a standard user becoming admin/root), while horizontal escalation moves sideways to another account at the same level to access its data; attackers achieve this by logging in as someone else, brute-forcing credentials, or exploiting vulnerabilities such as misconfigurations, kernel flaws, or SUID binaries to escape into a higher-privilege shell.
Escalation is a distinct phase in the attack lifecycle that follows initial access and enables lateral movement, persistence, and data exfiltration.

SOC analysts prioritize detecting and closing escalation paths because a low-severity foothold becomes a full breach the moment the attacker gains privileged control, and vulnerability scans often flag the exact CVEs and configuration weaknesses that make escalation possible.
privilege escalation.exam: The exam tests distinguishing vertical from horizontal privilege escalation and recognizing that a chained low-severity vulnerability enabling escalation should be prioritized higher than its base CVSS score suggests.

explain: Authentication attacks target the login process to gain access without legitimate authorization, and the three you must know are password spraying, credential stuffing, and impersonation.

Password spraying tries a small list of common passwords against many accounts to stay under lockout thresholds, while credential stuffing takes username/password pairs leaked from one breach and replays them across many other sites, exploiting the fact that people reuse credentials.
Impersonation is broader: the attacker presents themselves as a legitimate user or entity, often by stealing or replaying valid login credentials or session tokens.

Analysts care because these attacks produce distinct telemetry (many accounts failing one password versus one account tried with many passwords versus successful logins from impossible-travel locations), and recognizing the pattern drives the right response such as enforcing MFA, monitoring for leaked-credential reuse, and tuning detection thresholds.
authentication attacks.exam: You will be asked to identify password spraying versus credential stuffing versus brute force from authentication-log symptoms and to recommend MFA and credential-monitoring as countermeasures.

explain: Impersonation is an attack in which the adversary assumes the identity of a trusted user, service, device, or organization to gain access or trick a target into an action they would not otherwise take.

It is carried out by stealing and replaying valid credentials or session tokens, spoofing a source address or email domain, or using stolen certificates so that the attacker's traffic or requests appear to originate from a legitimate party.
Because the attacker operates under valid-looking identity, their activity can bypass access controls and blend in with normal behavior, making it harder to detect than an obvious intrusion.

SOC analysts counter impersonation with strong authentication (MFA), mutual TLS and certificate validation, anomaly detection on user and entity behavior, and email authentication controls such as SPF, DKIM, and DMARC.
impersonation.exam: Impersonation appears as the correct term when a scenario describes an attacker acting under a legitimate identity, and as the threat that MFA, UEBA, and email authentication (SPF/DKIM/DMARC) are meant to mitigate.

explain: A man-in-the-middle (also called on-path) attack occurs when an attacker secretly positions themselves between two communicating parties, relaying and potentially altering the traffic while each side believes it is talking directly to the other.

Common techniques that enable it include ARP poisoning on a local network, rogue or evil-twin Wi-Fi access points, DNS spoofing, and SSL stripping to downgrade an encrypted session to cleartext, all of which let the attacker intercept credentials, session tokens, and sensitive data.
The attack breaks the confidentiality and integrity of the channel because the adversary can both read and modify messages in transit.
Analysts defend against it with end-to-end encryption, certificate pinning and validation, HSTS to prevent downgrade, and network monitoring for signs of ARP or DNS manipulation.
man-in-the-middle (mitm) attack.exam: The exam expects you to recognize MITM/on-path from indicators like ARP poisoning, rogue access points, or SSL stripping, and to select encryption and certificate validation as the defenses.

explain: Session hijacking is an attack in which the adversary takes over an authenticated user's active session by obtaining that session's identifier, usually the session cookie or token, and then acting as the user without needing their password.

The token is captured by sniffing unencrypted traffic, stealing it through cross-site scripting, predicting a weak session ID, or fixing a known ID onto the victim (session fixation), after which the attacker replays it to inherit the victim's authenticated state.
It is dangerous precisely because it sidesteps the login and MFA that already happened, granting the attacker the user's privileges directly.

Analysts mitigate it by transmitting cookies only over TLS with the Secure and HttpOnly flags, regenerating session IDs after login, binding sessions to context, and enforcing timeouts, and they watch for a single session appearing from two locations.
session hijack.exam: Session hijacking questions test the role of the session token/cookie and the mitigations (HttpOnly/Secure cookies, session ID regeneration, TLS) that prevent token theft and replay.

explain: Cross-site scripting is a web vulnerability in which an attacker injects malicious client-side script (typically JavaScript) into a web page that other users then load, causing their browsers to execute the attacker's code in the context of the trusted site.

The three types are stored/persistent XSS (the payload is saved on the server, such as in a comment, and served to every viewer), reflected XSS (the payload is echoed back from a request, usually via a crafted link), and DOM-based XSS (the injection happens entirely in the browser's page script); all stem from failing to validate input and encode output.
A successful XSS attack can steal session cookies, log keystrokes, redirect users, or perform actions as the victim.

Analysts care because XSS is a persistent top web risk that feeds session hijacking and account takeover, and remediation centers on input validation, context-aware output encoding, and a Content Security Policy.
cross-site scripting (xss).exam: Expect questions distinguishing stored, reflected, and DOM-based XSS and identifying output encoding, input validation, and CSP as the correct mitigations.

explain: A rootkit is a stealthy form of malware designed to gain and maintain privileged (root/administrator) access to a system while hiding its own presence and the presence of other malicious processes, files, and network connections.

Rootkits operate at different levels: user-mode rootkits hook application APIs, kernel-mode rootkits modify the operating system core to falsify what tools report, and the most severe firmware/bootkit variants live in the BIOS/UEFI or boot loader so they persist beneath the OS and survive reinstallation.
Because they subvert the very system calls that monitoring tools rely on, a compromised host can report itself as clean while remaining fully controlled by the attacker.

Analysts treat rootkits as a high-severity persistence mechanism, detecting them with integrity checking, behavioral and memory analysis, secure/measured boot, and out-of-band verification, and often the safest remediation is to rebuild the system from known-good media.
rootkit.exam: The exam tests recognizing a rootkit from symptoms of hidden processes and integrity subversion, understanding kernel/firmware persistence, and knowing that reimaging is often the required remediation.

explain: Beyond injection, several common software weaknesses arise from insecure coding practices, including improper error handling, dereferencing, and insecure object references.

Improper error handling occurs when messages reveal too much internal detail (stack traces, file paths, database structure) that helps an attacker map the system, or when an unhandled error crashes the program instead of failing gracefully; the fix is to log full detail internally but return only a generic message to the user.

A dereferencing flaw happens when code follows a pointer or object reference to memory that is no longer valid (a null or dangling pointer), causing crashes or exploitable behavior, so references must be validated before use.

Insecure object referencing (insecure direct object reference, IDOR) exposes an internal identifier (such as a record or account ID) that an attacker can manipulate to access another user's data because the application fails to check authorization on each request; analysts flag these because they lead to information disclosure, denial of service, and unauthorized data access.
vulnerabilities.exam: Expect questions matching a described symptom (verbose error messages, null-pointer crash, an ID that can be changed to view another user's record) to the correct weakness and its secure-coding remedy such as generic errors, pointer validation, and per-request authorization checks.

explain: Regulatory and standards frameworks define the security and privacy obligations an organization must meet, and they directly drive which vulnerabilities must be remediated and how quickly.

Key ones include ISO/IEC 27001 (an international standard for building an information security management system), PCI-DSS (mandatory controls for any organization that stores, processes, or transmits payment card data), HIPAA (protection of U.S. protected health information), and GDPR (the EU regulation governing personal data with strict breach notification and heavy fines).
Internally, corporate policy and data classification determine how information is labeled and protected, translating external mandates into enforceable rules.

Analysts care because compliance requirements set remediation priorities and timelines (for example PCI-DSS mandates regular scanning and remediation of high-risk findings), so a vulnerability affecting regulated data often outranks one with a higher raw CVSS score.
regulatory environments.exam: The exam expects you to match each framework to its scope (PCI-DSS to cardholder data, HIPAA to health data, GDPR to EU personal data, ISO/IEC 27001 to the ISMS) and to recognize that compliance context influences vulnerability prioritization.

explain: Vulnerability identification is the process of discovering weaknesses across an environment, and it starts with a complete and accurate asset inventory because you cannot assess what you do not know exists (all endpoints, servers, network devices, cloud instances, and web applications).

Each asset must be assigned a criticality rating based on the data it holds and its business importance, since that rating (combined with exposure and exploitability) drives remediation priority rather than treating every finding equally.

Scanning can be active (the scanner sends probes and interacts with targets, giving detailed results but generating traffic and some risk to fragile systems) or passive (it observes existing network traffic without sending packets, which is safer and continuous but less complete), and specialized web-application scanning is needed to find flaws like injection and XSS that infrastructure scanners miss.
Analysts rely on this discipline so their limited remediation effort is focused on the vulnerabilities that most threaten the most important assets.
vulnerability identification.exam: Expect questions on why asset inventory and asset criticality underpin prioritization, and on choosing active versus passive scanning based on the need for depth versus the risk of disrupting sensitive systems.

explain: Mapping and enumeration is the reconnaissance stage in which an analyst or attacker discovers which hosts are alive, which ports and services they expose, and how the network is structured, forming the foundation for any vulnerability assessment.

Common host-discovery and probing techniques include ICMP echo requests (ping), TCP SYN scans to service ports such as 443, TCP ACK probes to ports like 80 to map firewall rules, and ICMP timestamp requests, each of which elicits responses that reveal whether a host or service is reachable.
Nmap is the standard tool for this work, combining host discovery, port scanning, service and version detection, and OS fingerprinting in one utility.

Analysts care because accurate mapping defines the true attack surface that scanning and remediation must cover, and recognizing these same probes in logs helps them detect an adversary's own reconnaissance.
mapping/ enumeration.exam: The exam tests identifying enumeration techniques (ICMP, TCP SYN/ACK probes) and knowing that Nmap performs host discovery, port scanning, and service/OS fingerprinting to establish the attack surface.

explain: Certification is the formal technical evaluation of a system or component to confirm that its security controls are correctly implemented and meet a defined baseline, whether that baseline is an internal organizational standard or an external regulatory requirement such as FISMA, PCI DSS, or a framework like NIST SP 800-53. It is a hands-on, evidence-based process in which assessors test and document how well the technical safeguards actually perform against the required criteria before the system is trusted for production use.

Accreditation, by contrast, is the managerial decision in which a senior authorizing official reviews the certification results and formally accepts the system, along with any residual risk, for operation in a specific environment. Where certification answers the technical question of whether the controls work, accreditation answers the business question of whether the organization is willing to accept the remaining risk given its mission and business model, and it is this sign-off that grants the authorization to operate.

For a SOC or security analyst, certification and accreditation define which systems are approved to run and under what conditions, so findings, vulnerabilities, and control gaps you report can jeopardize a system's authorization and must be communicated clearly to the authorizing official. Understanding the split also clarifies escalation: technical remediation and evidence flow up through certification, while acceptance of residual risk is a management responsibility you inform but do not own.
certification & accreditation.exam: On the CySA+ exam, expect questions that ask you to distinguish certification (the technical assessment of controls) from accreditation (management's formal risk acceptance and authorization to operate), often in the context of reporting findings to stakeholders and supporting the authorization decision.

explain: Storage encryption protects data at rest so that if a drive or device is lost, stolen, or improperly decommissioned, the stored contents remain unreadable without the decryption key. The most common form is full-disk encryption (FDE), which encrypts the entire volume including the operating system, page file, and temporary files.

FDE can be implemented in software, where the operating system or a product such as BitLocker or LUKS performs the cryptographic operations using the host CPU, or in hardware, where the drive itself performs encryption transparently. Software FDE is flexible and low-cost but consumes CPU cycles and depends on the OS being trustworthy, while hardware encryption offloads the work and keeps keys off the general-purpose processor.

A security analyst cares because encrypting storage is a primary defense-in-depth control for confidentiality and is often a compliance requirement, and because understanding the implementation determines the real-world attack surface and recovery options.
storage encryption.exam: Expect questions asking you to compare software-based FDE against hardware-based encryption and to identify which control protects data at rest on a lost or stolen device.

explain: Hardware encryption performs cryptographic operations on a dedicated controller rather than on the host CPU, most commonly implemented as a self-encrypting drive (SED) that encrypts and decrypts every block transparently as data moves to and from the platters or flash. The drive always encrypts the media with an internal data-encryption key, so encryption is effectively always on.

The user supplies a password or passphrase, but that password is not used directly to scramble the data; instead it is used to encrypt (wrap) the drive's media-encryption key, and the resulting encrypted key is stored in nonvolatile memory inside the disk controller. This design lets an administrator perform a near-instant cryptographic erase by discarding the media key, and it lets the password be changed without re-encrypting the entire drive.

An analyst cares because SEDs offload work from the CPU, resist software-based key extraction better than pure software FDE, and support rapid sanitization, but the plaintext is still exposed in memory once data is read, which shapes the residual risk.
hardware encryption.exam: The exam tests whether you understand that a self-encrypting drive stores an encrypted media key in the controller and that the user password unlocks that key rather than being the key itself.

explain: Bus encryption addresses a gap in self-encrypting drives, where data is decrypted to plaintext at the disk controller and then travels across the internal data bus in the clear, exposing it to bus-probing or memory-snooping attacks. It moves the cryptographic module off the disk controller and closer to or inside the CPU so that data remains ciphertext while it is on the bus and is only decrypted within a protected boundary.

This approach requires a dedicated cryptoprocessor chip that decrypts instructions and data only inside a trusted boundary, meaning software must be specifically compiled or provisioned to run in that protected environment. Because of that requirement it imposes real functional limitations and cannot run arbitrary off-the-shelf software.

Bus encryption is expensive, complex, and restrictive, so it is used for high-assurance embedded and special-purpose systems rather than general-purpose computers; an analyst should recognize it as a strong but niche control when evaluating protection of data in transit inside a machine.
bus encryption.exam: Look for questions contrasting bus encryption with SEDs, noting that bus encryption keeps data as ciphertext on the data bus and is impractical for general-purpose computers due to cost and complexity.

explain: Secure processing provides a hardware-backed protected runtime that isolates sensitive code and data from the main operating system and other applications, so that even a compromised OS cannot read or tamper with what runs inside it. This is typically delivered as a trusted execution environment (TEE) or a secure enclave carved out of the main processor.

A TEE is a runtime environment that limits how programs interact with one another and with the outside world, enforcing confidentiality and integrity for the code and data loaded into it, and reputable implementations undergo rigorous assessment prior to certification so their isolation guarantees can be trusted. Common uses include protecting cryptographic keys, biometric templates, digital-rights material, and attestation secrets.

An analyst cares because secure enclaves shrink the attack surface for the most sensitive operations and support hardware root-of-trust and remote attestation, which are increasingly relied on for verifying system integrity and protecting credentials.
secure processing.exam: Expect items describing a trusted execution environment or secure enclave and asking why an isolated runtime protects sensitive operations such as key handling from the main OS.

explain: A processor that supports secure processing effectively runs two worlds side by side: the rich execution environment (REE), where the normal operating system and general applications run, and the trusted execution environment (TEE), where isolated, protected code runs shielded from the REE. Sensitive workloads are placed in the TEE precisely because the REE is large, exposed, and cannot be fully trusted.

The separation is enforced by processor security extensions, which are additional CPU instructions and hardware modes such as Intel SGX or Arm TrustZone that support TEE functionality by controlling when execution transitions between the secure and non-secure worlds and by restricting the REE's access to TEE memory. Without these hardware extensions, software isolation alone could not resist a compromised kernel.

An analyst cares because knowing whether a platform provides a genuine hardware TEE versus only software isolation determines how much assurance can be placed in on-device key storage, attestation, and other security-critical functions.
tee and ree.exam: The exam may ask you to distinguish the trusted execution environment from the rich execution environment and to identify processor security extensions as the CPU instructions that enable that separation.

explain: Trusted Foundry is a U.S. Department of Defense program that certifies semiconductor manufacturers so that the supply chain for DoD mission-critical systems is hardened against tampering, counterfeiting, and the insertion of malicious logic or backdoors during chip fabrication. It gives the government assurance that microelectronics in weapons and other critical platforms come from vetted, secure sources.

The certification process is rigorous, covering the security and integrity of design, fabrication, packaging, and handling, and fewer than 100 companies have passed it to be designated as trusted foundries. This deliberate scarcity reflects how demanding the assurance requirements are.

A security analyst cares because hardware supply-chain integrity is a growing threat vector, and the Trusted Foundry concept illustrates how organizations manage the risk that vulnerabilities or implants could be introduced at the manufacturing layer, below the reach of software controls.
trusted foundry.exam: Expect a supply-chain question identifying the Trusted Foundry program as a DoD initiative that vets a small number of certified manufacturers to prevent tampered or counterfeit microelectronics.

explain: Anti-tamper techniques are physical and design defenses that protect a chip's secrets from adversaries who have physical possession of the hardware and attempt to extract keys or reverse-engineer logic. Attackers use chip attacks such as microprobing, which applies voltage to internal conductors and records the results to read out data, and visual analysis, which carefully removes the chip's covering layer by layer to photograph and map the circuitry.

To thwart these, chip manufacturers employ countermeasures such as emitting random signals to confuse microprobing so the attacker cannot correlate probe readings, and building tamper-detection meshes or sensors that detect when the chip's casing or die coating is compromised. When such tampering is detected, the chip can immediately place zeros into its nonvolatile memory, destroying stored keys before they can be extracted.

An analyst cares because tamper resistance underpins the trust placed in HSMs, smart cards, secure enclaves, and other cryptographic hardware, and knowing these defenses clarifies why physical access does not automatically defeat well-designed key storage.
anti-tamper techniques.exam: Look for questions describing physical chip attacks such as microprobing or layer-by-layer decapsulation and asking which countermeasures zeroize secrets or generate noise to defeat them.

explain: Attack frameworks provide a common, structured language for describing how adversaries operate, helping teams define the tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) an attacker uses so that defenders can detect, communicate about, and respond to threats consistently. The most widely used is MITRE ATT&CK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques, and Common Knowledge), a curated knowledge base maintained by the MITRE Corporation and built from observed real-world adversary behavior.

ATT&CK organizes behavior into tactics, the attacker's objectives, which for the enterprise matrix include categories such as discovery, lateral movement, defense evasion, credential access, and collection, each populated with specific techniques that describe how the objective is achieved. Analysts map alerts and telemetry to these tactics and techniques to understand where in an intrusion they are and what may come next.

A SOC analyst cares because ATT&CK drives detection engineering, threat hunting, coverage gap analysis, and threat-intelligence enrichment, letting the team measure defenses against how adversaries actually behave rather than against isolated indicators.
attack frameworks.exam: The exam frequently references MITRE ATT&CK as a knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques and asks you to map observed activity such as lateral movement or defense evasion to it.

explain: The Diamond Model of Intrusion Analysis structures every malicious event around four core features arranged as the points of a diamond: adversary, capability, infrastructure, and victim. Its foundational axiom is that for every intrusion event there exists an adversary taking a step toward some goal by using a capability over infrastructure against a victim, so these four elements are always present and connected.

The model links the points with meta-features such as timestamp, phase, result, direction, and methodology, and it emphasizes that pivoting from any one vertex can reveal the others, for example moving from an observed piece of infrastructure to the capability delivered through it or to other victims it touched. This makes analysis a process of discovering and correlating related events rather than examining indicators in isolation.

An analyst cares because the Diamond Model organizes threat intelligence and correlates activity across intrusions, and it pairs well with kill-chain and ATT&CK thinking to attribute campaigns and anticipate adversary behavior.
diamond model axioms.exam: Expect questions identifying the Diamond Model's four core features and its central axiom that every intrusion event links an adversary and a victim through a capability and infrastructure.

explain: The Lockheed Martin Cyber Kill Chain is a model that breaks an intrusion into seven sequential phases: reconnaissance, weaponization, delivery, exploitation, installation, command and control (C2), and actions on objectives. It frames an attack as a chain in which the adversary must complete each stage to reach their goal, so breaking any link disrupts the overall attack.

In practice defenders map controls and detections to each phase, aiming to detect or deny the adversary as early as possible, because stopping delivery or exploitation is far cheaper and safer than reacting after the attacker has established C2 or begun exfiltration during actions on objectives. The model also encourages layering defenses so multiple opportunities exist to break the chain.

A SOC analyst cares because the kill chain guides detection coverage, incident scoping, and course-of-action planning, though analysts should recognize its linearity is a limitation and often combine it with ATT&CK, which better captures non-linear, real-world techniques.
lockheed martin cyber kill chain.exam: Look for questions asking you to place an observed action in the correct kill-chain phase or to explain how disrupting an early stage such as delivery stops the intrusion before actions on objectives.

explain: Effective incident response depends on clearly defined roles that ensure the right authority, knowledge, and support are available when an incident occurs. Senior leaders must be included in the decision-making process because their visibility and support secure resources, help address regulatory and legal obligations, and provide the authority to make hard containment decisions.

Leadership and dedicated coordinators also act as a buffer between the technical IR team and other personnel or executives, shielding responders from distraction so they can work while keeping stakeholders appropriately informed. Team composition should be scaled to the scope of the incident, bringing in the right knowledge and experience to meet the specific problem, and any outside resources such as forensic firms or legal counsel need coordination and pre-set parameters like retainers and contact procedures so they can be engaged quickly.

An analyst cares because these roles and an agreed escalation path for escalated IR determine how smoothly a response runs under pressure, and gaps in sponsorship or unclear authority are a common reason incidents are handled slowly or incorrectly.
ir process key roles.exam: Expect questions on who must be involved in incident response, especially the value of senior-leadership sponsorship, defined escalation, and coordinating outside resources under pre-set parameters.

explain: Organizations structure their incident response or CSIRT capability in one of three common models depending on their size, geography, and resources. A central response team is a single team that addresses incidents as they come up across the whole organization, and it works well for smaller or single-site organizations because coordination is simple and expertise is consolidated.

A distributed response team is used by larger organizations and consists of geographically or business-unit separate teams that handle incidents in their own areas while coordinating under shared processes, providing local coverage and time-zone reach at the cost of tighter coordination requirements. An outsourced response team is provided by an outside organization that responds to incidents as a service, letting a company obtain specialized skills and around-the-clock coverage without maintaining full in-house staff.

An analyst cares because the chosen structure shapes response times, escalation paths, and where authority and knowledge reside, and many organizations blend these models, keeping a small internal team that engages an outsourced provider for surge capacity or specialized forensics.
team structure.exam: The exam asks you to match an organization's size and geography to the appropriate CSIRT model — central, distributed, or outsourced — and to know their respective trade-offs.

explain: A Business Impact Analysis (BIA) is a structured study that identifies an organization's critical business functions and the maximum tolerable downtime and disruption each can withstand before the harm becomes unacceptable.

It weighs multiple impact dimensions for each function: operational disruption and lost productivity, direct and indirect financial losses, regulatory and legal responsibilities that a disruption would breach, and damage to the organization's reputation and customer trust.
The BIA feeds recovery objectives such as the Recovery Time Objective (RTO) and Recovery Point Objective (RPO) that drive continuity and disaster-recovery planning.

A SOC or security analyst relies on the BIA to prioritize which assets and services to protect and restore first, so incident response and resource allocation are aligned to what actually keeps the business running.
business impact analysis.exam: Expect scenario questions asking you to determine which system to recover or protect first based on maximum tolerable downtime and business criticality identified in a BIA.

explain: A BIA follows a repeatable process that begins by selecting interviewees from all organizational levels, then choosing data-gathering techniques such as surveys, questionnaires, and both qualitative and quantitative approaches to collect consistent information.

The analyst then identifies the company's critical business functions, the resources (people, systems, data, suppliers) those functions depend on, and calculates how long each function can survive without those resources.
Next the team identifies the vulnerabilities and threats to each critical function and calculates the resulting risk, so the most exposed functions are clearly ranked.
Finally the findings are documented and reported to management with recommendations, giving decision-makers the evidence to fund controls and set recovery priorities.
business impact analysis steps.exam: Questions may present the BIA steps out of order or ask what happens at a specific stage, so know that resource-dependency and survival-time analysis precede risk calculation and the management report.

explain: Risk identification is the phase of risk management whose main goals are to identify vulnerabilities, determine the probability that a threat will exploit each vulnerability, and estimate the potential business impact of each threat.
It also seeks an economic balance between the impact of a threat and the cost of the countermeasure, so an organization does not spend more defending an asset than the asset is worth.

Analysts drive the work by asking the right questions: what event could occur (the threat event), what its potential impact would be (magnitude), how likely it is to happen (probability), and how confident they are in those answers (certainty).
For a security analyst this framing turns vague concerns into structured, defensible inputs that support consistent prioritization and reporting to management.
risk identification.exam: The exam tests the four guiding questions—threat event, magnitude, probability, and certainty—and the principle that countermeasure cost should not exceed the value of the asset it protects.

explain: The risk identification process gathers risk inputs from multiple sources: evaluating cyber threat intelligence, conducting vulnerability assessments, observing day-to-day cybersecurity operations, and organizing brainstorming sessions with stakeholders.
Identified risks are captured in a risk register, the central document that tracks each risk throughout its lifecycle.
Each register entry typically records a unique identifier, a short name, a description, an assigned owner responsible for managing it, and a probability rating (often alongside impact).
A SOC analyst uses the risk register as a living, auditable record that keeps risks visible, assigns accountability, and drives follow-up and treatment decisions.
risk identification process.exam: Know the standard fields of a risk register (ID, name, description, owner, probability/impact) and recognize threat intel, vulnerability assessments, and brainstorming as valid risk-identification inputs.

explain: Risk calculation quantifies or ranks identified risks using two complementary methods: qualitative analysis, which rates risk on descriptive scales like high/medium/low, and quantitative analysis, which assigns numeric values such as SLE, ARO, and ALE in monetary terms.
Whichever method is used, the risks that must be mitigated first are those with the highest probability of occurring combined with the highest magnitude of impact.

The Delphi technique supports qualitative estimation by having each participant anonymously list risks and anonymously comment, removing groupthink and dominant-personality bias so the consensus reflects independent expert judgment.
Analysts care because a defensible calculation determines where limited budget and effort go, and anonymity in Delphi produces more honest input than open discussion.
risk calculation.exam: Distinguish qualitative (subjective scales) from quantitative (numeric/monetary, e.g. ALE = SLE × ARO) analysis, and recognize the Delphi technique by its anonymous, iterative expert consensus.

explain: A qualitative risk matrix (heat map) is a grid that plots each risk's likelihood on one axis against its impact on the other to produce an overall severity rating without exact numbers.
The intersecting cells are usually color-coded—commonly green for low, yellow for moderate, and red for high or critical—so priorities are visible at a glance.
Because it relies on descriptive ratings rather than dollar figures, the matrix is fast to build and easy for non-technical audiences to interpret.
Security analysts use it to communicate relative risk priority to management quickly and to justify which risks warrant immediate treatment.
qualitative risk matrix.exam: Expect to read a likelihood-versus-impact matrix and identify which risk falls in the highest-severity (red) cell and therefore should be addressed first.

explain: Communicating risk factors means presenting risk findings to multiple audiences, from executives and boards to technical teams and external partners, each of whom needs the information framed differently.

The message must be tailored for each audience: leadership needs business impact, cost, and risk-appetite language, while technical staff need specific vulnerabilities, affected systems, and remediation detail.
Effective communication translates technical findings into terms that let each group make appropriate decisions and take the right action.
For a SOC analyst, poorly tailored reporting stalls remediation and funding, so matching content, depth, and vocabulary to the audience is a core professional skill.
communication of risk factors.exam: Questions test choosing the right report content and level of technical detail for a given audience, such as an executive summary for the board versus a detailed finding for engineers.

explain: Teaming assigns exercise roles by color: the Red Team acts as the opposing force (OPFOR) simulating real threat actors to validate the defenders' assumptions, while the Blue Team is the defenders who detect, respond to, and fix what the Red Team discovers.
The White Team plans and moderates the exercise, sets the rules of engagement, and adjudicates the outcome as a neutral referee.

The Purple Team is a dynamic hybrid that has Red and Blue work together collaboratively, testing the Blue Team's people, processes, and technologies while sharing techniques in real time rather than in secret.
Analysts benefit because purple teaming closes the feedback loop fastest, turning offensive findings directly into improved detections and defenses.
teaming.exam: Be able to match each team color to its role, especially that Purple Team means Red and Blue collaborating and White Team means the neutral planners and moderators.

explain: Building analyst capability combines formal technical training with real-life experience and active participation in the security community, such as giving presentations at security conferences to sharpen and share expertise.

Hands-on rehearsal comes through tabletop exercises (TTXs), which are discussion-based walkthroughs of an incident scenario, and live-fire exercises, which test teams against active simulated attacks.

A cyber range provides a safe, isolated virtual environment where defenders can practice detection and response against realistic attacks without risking production systems, and organizations may stand up separate training teams to run these programs.
A SOC values these resources because skills degrade without practice, and rehearsing under realistic conditions exposes gaps in people, process, and tooling before a real incident does.
training programs & resources.exam: Distinguish a tabletop exercise (discussion-based) from a live-fire exercise (hands-on simulated attack) and recognize a cyber range as the isolated environment used for realistic practice.

explain: Vendor due diligence is the investigation an organization performs before and after engaging a third party to confirm the vendor can be trusted with its data and operations.

It includes reviewing references and speaking with former and current customers, checking sources such as Better Business Bureau (BBB) reports, and ensuring contracts require adequate security controls and that service level agreements (SLAs) define performance and availability commitments.

Deeper assurance comes from reviewing the vendor's security program, its internal and external audit reports and third-party reviews, conducting onsite inspections and interviews after signing, and confirming the vendor maintains a business continuity plan (BCP), backed by a nondisclosure agreement (NDA) to protect shared information.
Analysts care because third-party weaknesses become the organization's own risk, and diligence provides contractual and evidentiary leverage to hold vendors to a security baseline.
vendor due diligence.exam: Expect questions on evaluating third-party risk, recognizing SLAs, NDAs, BCP requirements, and audit-report review as the mechanisms that enforce vendor security.

explain: Supply chain risk assessment evaluates the threats introduced by the hardware, software, and services an organization sources from others, since a compromise anywhere upstream can reach the buyer.

A central concern is hardware source authenticity—verifying that components are genuine and have not been counterfeited or tampered with (for example, implanted backdoors) during manufacturing or transit.
The U.S. Department of Defense addresses this with the Trusted Foundry program, which certifies suppliers to produce microelectronics through a vetted, secure, and controlled process.
A security analyst assesses supply chain risk because counterfeit or tampered components can defeat every downstream control, making provenance and trusted sourcing part of the overall risk posture.
supply chain risk assessment.exam: Recognize hardware source authenticity and the DoD Trusted Foundry program as controls that counter counterfeit and tampered components in the supply chain.

explain: The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) publishes widely adopted cybersecurity guidance, including its Special Publication series that defines security control catalogs and processes.

NIST SP 800-53 provides a comprehensive catalog of recommended security and privacy controls for federal information systems and organizations, and is broadly reused in the private sector as a control baseline.

The NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) offers a risk-based, outcome-oriented structure organized around core functions—Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, and Recover (with Govern added in CSF 2.0)—that maps controls to business objectives.
Security analysts use these publications to select controls, benchmark maturity, and speak a common language with auditors, regulators, and management.
nist.exam: Know that SP 800-53 is the control catalog and that the NIST CSF is organized around its core functions (Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover, and Govern in CSF 2.0).

explain: The communications process defines who may know about an incident, how information about it is shared, and through what secure channels, so that response is coordinated while leaks and premature disclosure are prevented. A trusted core group, sometimes called the circle of trust, is kept deliberately small and operates on a need-to-know basis, expanding only to the key internal staff and external partners (legal counsel, law enforcement, regulators, PR, third-party responders) that each stage of the response actually requires.

Disclosure timing and audience are often dictated by regulatory or legislative requirements, such as breach-notification laws that impose deadlines for informing affected individuals and authorities, so the plan must specify what is said, to whom, and when. Out-of-band, encrypted communication channels are used because an attacker who has compromised email or chat could otherwise read the response team's messages, and a clear policy governs what employees are and are not permitted to say about the incident to limit rumor, reputational damage, and evidence contamination.

A SOC analyst cares because a technically sound response can still fail legally or reputationally if information flows to the wrong people, tips off the attacker, or violates a mandatory notification window.
communications process.exam: Expect scenario questions asking who should be notified, when regulatory disclosure is required, or why the team must use secure out-of-band channels and enforce need-to-know.

explain: Responsibilities and coordination mean that every role in the incident response effort is clearly defined and documented in advance, so that when an incident occurs each person knows exactly what they are accountable for rather than improvising under pressure. The assignments must be understandable and unambiguous, covering the incident commander, technical responders, communications lead, legal and management liaisons, and any external partners, so handoffs are clean and no critical task is left owner-less.

The plan should also be portable, meaning it is accessible and usable across teams, locations, and even when primary systems or key personnel are unavailable, for example through printed copies or an out-of-band store that survives a network outage. Coordination ties these roles together so parallel workstreams such as containment, evidence collection, and stakeholder updates progress without conflict or duplication.

SOC analysts rely on this clarity to escalate correctly and act within their authority, because confusion over who is in charge or who can approve actions like isolating a system directly slows response and increases damage.
responsibilities & coordination.exam: Questions test knowing which role performs a given action or approves an escalation, and why documented, portable role assignments matter during an active incident.

explain: Preparation is the first phase of incident response and the only one that aims to prevent incidents from happening in the first place, rather than reacting after the fact. It is built on three pillars: people (trained staff, defined roles, awareness), process (documented policies, playbooks, and communication plans), and technology (the tools, monitoring, and defensive controls that support the team).

Concrete preparation activities include network and host hardening, such as disabling unnecessary services, enforcing least privilege, and configuring secure baselines, together with disciplined patch and update management to close known vulnerabilities before they are exploited. It also means having the response toolkit, jump kits, contact lists, and logging in place and tested before an incident, not scrambling to assemble them mid-crisis.

A security analyst cares because the quality of preparation directly determines how fast and effectively the team can detect, contain, and recover; weak preparation turns a minor event into a major breach.
preparation.exam: Expect items identifying preparation activities (hardening, patching, playbooks, training) and recognizing preparation as the proactive NIST phase distinct from detection or containment.

explain: Active security measures center on knowing your own attack surface, meaning the complete set of points where an attacker could attempt to enter, interact with, or extract data from a system. Attack surface analysis is the practice of enumerating those exposed elements, such as open ports, exposed APIs, web forms, user inputs, network services, and trust boundaries, so the organization understands where it is reachable.

The main goal is to identify the key parts of a system that must be tested for vulnerabilities and then reduce or defend that exposure, which lets the security team anticipate likely attack paths and prioritize protection of the most critical assets. The same insight helps developers build more secure products by minimizing unnecessary exposure and validating the inputs attackers would target.
SOC analysts care because you cannot monitor or defend what you have not mapped, and an unmanaged or growing attack surface is where breaches most often originate.
active security measures.exam: Expect questions on identifying an organization's attack surface and on how attack surface reduction proactively lowers exploitable exposure before an incident.

explain: Attack surface analysis is a structured review, typically performed by security architects and penetration testers, that maps every avenue through which an adversary could reach or affect a system. It systematically identifies which parts of a system should be reviewed and tested for vulnerabilities and pinpoints the high-risk areas, such as internet-facing services, authentication endpoints, and privileged interfaces, that most need defensive attention.

A critical output is recognizing when the attack surface changes, for example after deploying a new service, opening a firewall rule, adding a cloud workload, or integrating a third party, since each change can introduce fresh exposure that existing controls do not cover. Comparing the current surface against a known baseline reveals this drift.

A security analyst uses attack surface analysis to focus scanning, monitoring, and hardening on the areas of greatest exposure and to trigger reassessment whenever the environment shifts, keeping defenses aligned with reality rather than an outdated snapshot.
attack surface analysis.exam: Questions ask who conducts attack surface analysis, what it identifies, and why a change in the attack surface should prompt renewed testing and monitoring.

explain: This concept covers indicators of compromise (IoCs), the observable forensic artifacts that suggest a system may be under attack or already breached, which analysts learn to recognize during the detection and analysis phase. Common network and account signs include unusual outbound traffic, anomalous privileged or admin account activity, geographic irregularities such as logins from impossible-travel locations, and login irregularities like repeated failed attempts or off-hours access.

Data-focused indicators include a spike in database read volume or an unusually large HTML response size, both of which can signal bulk data exfiltration, along with a high number of requests against the same file, which may indicate brute-forcing or scraping. Host and protocol indicators include mismatched port-to-application traffic, where a service runs on an unexpected port to evade detection, and suspicious changes to the registry or system files that point to persistence or tampering.

A SOC analyst memorizes these patterns because early, accurate recognition of IoCs is what separates a contained incident from a full-scale breach, and correlating several weak signals often reveals an attack that any single alert would miss.
detection & analysis \u2013 know the sig.exam: Expect scenarios listing observed behavior (e.g., large outbound transfers, off-hours admin logins, mismatched port traffic) and asking you to identify it as an indicator of compromise.

explain: Detection and analysis is the NIST phase in which the team recognizes that an incident is occurring and determines its nature, scope, and severity, and its effectiveness depends on preparing reliable data sources in advance. Central to this is a SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) platform, which aggregates and correlates logs from across the environment so that related events are surfaced as a single actionable alert rather than scattered noise.

Supporting sources include IDS/IPS sensors that flag or block known malicious network patterns, and the broad collection of alerts and logs from endpoints, firewalls, servers, and applications that provide the raw evidence for investigation. Well-tuned alerting reduces false positives so analysts can focus on genuine threats.

A security analyst cares because you can only respond to what you can see; comprehensive, correlated, and properly retained log data is the foundation for validating an alert, reconstructing an attacker's actions, and scoping the incident accurately.
detection & analysis.exam: Questions test the role of the SIEM in correlating logs, the function of IDS/IPS, and why source preparation and log collection underpin the detection and analysis phase.

explain: Determining severity is the process of assessing an incident's business impact so responders can prioritize effort and escalate appropriately, rather than treating every event as equally urgent. Key dimensions include the scope of impact (how many systems, users, and services are affected), downtime measured against the maximum tolerable downtime the business can absorb, and recovery time, since prolonged outages translate directly into lost revenue on the principle that time is money.

Severity also weighs data integrity, meaning whether information has been tampered with or deleted, the economic impact reflecting the value and replacement cost of affected assets, and business process criticality, which asks how essential the disrupted function is to core operations. An incident hitting a revenue-generating or safety-critical process ranks far higher than one affecting a non-essential system.

A SOC analyst uses these factors to assign a priority that drives resource allocation and escalation, ensuring the most damaging incidents get immediate attention while lower-impact ones are handled proportionally.
determining severity.exam: Expect questions asking you to rank or prioritize incidents based on scope, downtime tolerance, data integrity, economic cost, and criticality of the affected business process.

explain: Understanding types of data matters because the classification and sensitivity of the information involved drive an incident's severity, notification obligations, and legal exposure. Regulated personal data includes PHI (Protected Health Information), governed by health-privacy laws, and PII (Personally Identifiable Information) that can identify an individual, both of which typically trigger mandatory breach-notification requirements when exposed.

Payment card information falls under contractual standards such as PCI DSS, while corporate secrets and intellectual property, including patents, trademarks and copyright, trade secrets, accounting records, and merger-and-acquisition plans, represent high-value competitive and financial assets. Loss of any of these carries distinct regulatory, financial, or strategic consequences.

A security analyst identifies which data types are affected early in an incident because that determination dictates how severely the incident is rated, which regulators and stakeholders must be told, and how urgently containment must proceed.
types of data.exam: Questions test recognizing data classifications such as PHI, PII, and payment card data and matching a breach to the regulatory or notification obligations those data types impose.

explain: Knowing your threat means understanding the specific vulnerabilities, assets, and adversaries relevant to your organization so defenses and response are grounded in reality rather than generic assumptions. This requires answering three questions: what type of data you hold and therefore what an attacker would want, what your systems actually look like in terms of architecture and exposure, and who the likely threat actors are, from opportunistic criminals to organized crime, hacktivists, insiders, and nation-state groups.

Because different threat actors have different motivations, capabilities, and techniques, profiling them lets the team anticipate the tactics they are most likely to use and align controls and monitoring accordingly. Awareness of the broader threat landscape and current vulnerabilities keeps this picture up to date.

A SOC analyst applies this knowledge to interpret alerts in context, prioritize the vulnerabilities most likely to be exploited against them, and tailor detection to the adversaries that genuinely pose a risk to their environment.
know your threat.exam: Expect questions on aligning defenses to threat actor type, data value, and system exposure, testing the link between threat intelligence and prioritized response.

explain: The incident response process is the structured lifecycle an organization follows to handle security incidents, and the authoritative reference on the exam is NIST Special Publication 800-61, the Computer Security Incident Handling Guide. NIST, the National Institute of Standards and Technology, is a U.S. federal body that publishes widely adopted technology standards and guidelines, and SP 800-61 defines the phases and best practices for building and running an incident response capability.

Following a recognized framework like SP 800-61 gives the team a repeatable, defensible methodology so that response is consistent, thorough, and aligned with industry expectations rather than ad hoc. It establishes common terminology and a shared sequence of steps that different teams and organizations can coordinate around.

A security analyst cares because CySA+ and most enterprise programs model their playbooks on this standard, so knowing its structure lets you slot activities into the correct phase and communicate clearly with the rest of the response team.
incident response (ir) process.exam: Expect direct recall that NIST SP 800-61 is the incident-handling guide and recognition of NIST as the standards body behind the IR framework.

explain: The incident response process is divided into distinct phases, and Phase I is Preparation, the proactive stage that readies the organization before any incident occurs. Its proactive measures include network segmentation, which limits how far an attacker can move laterally, and host hardening, which reduces the ways a system can be compromised, together forming the defensive baseline the rest of the process depends on.

Preparation also encompasses a formal risk assessment process to identify and rank vulnerabilities, predefined action steps and playbooks so responders know what to do, and established communication plans so the right people are informed through the right channels. It further sets up the activity logging and reporting mechanisms needed to document an incident and support later analysis.

A security analyst cares because everything the later phases of detection, containment, eradication, and recovery rely on, from segmented networks to ready playbooks to reliable logs, is put in place during Preparation, making it the foundation of an effective response.
incident response (ir) process phases.exam: Questions test identifying Preparation as the first NIST phase and recognizing its activities (segmentation, hardening, risk assessment, playbooks, communication planning) versus later phases.

explain: Mobile device forensics is the practice of acquiring and analyzing data from smartphones and tablets, which is often harder than disk forensics because the operating systems are closed and proprietary and the storage cannot be imaged as easily as a removable hard drive.

Because these devices constantly communicate with cellular, Wi-Fi, and Bluetooth networks, an attacker or owner can issue a remote-wipe or remote-lock command that alters or destroys evidence, so investigators isolate the device using a Faraday bag or Faraday cage that blocks all radio-frequency (RF) signaling.

Direct access to the device's data is typically not possible through the normal interface, so analysts rely on specialized mobile forensics hardware and software such as Cellebrite UFED or Magnet AXIOM to extract data through logical, file-system, or physical acquisition methods.

A SOC or forensic analyst cares because mobile devices hold rich evidence such as call logs, messages, location history, and app data, and losing that evidence to a remote wipe or an improper acquisition can break the case and the chain of custody.
mobile device forensics.exam: Expect scenario questions where an analyst must preserve a seized phone and choose a Faraday bag or specialized mobile forensic tooling to prevent remote wiping and maintain evidence integrity.

explain: When incidents occur on virtual machines or in cloud environments, the forensic approach shifts because the analyst rarely has physical access to the underlying host hardware and instead works with virtualized abstractions of storage, memory, and network.

Service Level Agreements (SLAs) and the cloud shared-responsibility model can legally and technically limit forensic activities, since the provider owns the hypervisor and physical layer and may not grant the tenant access to logs or disk images below the guest OS.

A key advantage of virtualization is the snapshot, which captures the complete state of a VM including its memory and disk at a point in time, and a properly taken and hashed snapshot can serve as forensically sound evidence preservation of the system as it existed during the incident.

Analysts care because they must plan acquisitions around what the provider will allow, request logs early, and capture snapshots quickly before auto-scaling or ephemeral instances destroy the evidence.
virtualization and the cloud.exam: Look for questions on how cloud SLAs and shared responsibility limit an analyst's access to underlying hardware, and how VM snapshots are used to capture forensically sound evidence.

explain: A legal hold is a formal, court-driven or counsel-driven obligation to preserve all data and evidence relevant to anticipated or ongoing litigation, suspending normal deletion and retention schedules so nothing potentially relevant is destroyed.

For evidence to be admissible in a court of law it must be shown to be in its original, unaltered state, and the legal hold ensures that state is maintained; the original evidence generally cannot be returned to its owner until the trial concludes.

Because keeping the physical original out of production is often impractical, a verified forensic image, one whose cryptographic hash matches the source and whose acquisition is documented, can suffice as forensically sound evidence in place of the original.

A security analyst cares because failing to honor a legal hold can lead to spoliation sanctions and destroyed evidence, so IR playbooks must trigger preservation and proper imaging the moment litigation is reasonably anticipated.
legal hold.exam: Expect questions distinguishing a legal hold obligation to preserve evidence from routine retention, and recognizing that verified forensic images can substitute for the original device during litigation.

explain: Manual forensic analysis means examining a system's operating system and running processes directly using log viewers and native artifacts rather than relying on an all-in-one commercial suite.

On Windows, key evidence sources include the Event Viewer, which holds the Security, System, and Application logs, and the Registry, which records installed software, user activity, run keys, and persistence mechanisms.

On Linux, analysts examine standard directories such as /etc/ for configuration files, /var/log/ for system and application logs like auth.log and syslog, and /home/ for per-user files, histories, and artifacts.
A SOC analyst cares because knowing exactly where artifacts live lets them quickly validate an alert, reconstruct attacker actions, and pull evidence even when specialized tooling is unavailable.
forensics analysis, i.exam: Look for questions asking where specific artifacts live, such as the Windows Registry and Event Viewer versus Linux paths like /var/log, /etc, and /home.

explain: Beyond manual review, analysts use dedicated forensic solutions to acquire, index, and analyze evidence at scale while preserving integrity and chain of custody.

Common commercial suites include AccessData FTK (Forensic Toolkit) and OpenText EnCase, while The Sleuth Kit (TSK) with its Autopsy front end is a widely used open-source alternative for file-system analysis.
These tools support timeline analysis, which correlates file metadata, log entries, and artifacts into a chronological sequence so an investigator can see the order of events during an incident.
A security analyst cares because these platforms speed up investigations, produce court-defensible reports, and surface patterns across large data sets that manual review would miss.
forensics analysis.exam: Expect questions naming commercial and open-source forensic suites (FTK, EnCase, The Sleuth Kit) and identifying timeline analysis as a core investigative technique.

explain: Timeline analysis searches across log files, file-system metadata, and other artifacts to build a single correlated chronological timeline that an investigator can easily read to reconstruct what happened and when.

When the exact time of the incident is unknown, analysts build a super timeline that aggregates every available timestamped artifact into one master view, commonly using the Plaso engine and its log2timeline tool.

When the time of the incident is known, analysts build a targeted timeline, taking snapshots of the system state pre-incident and post-incident so they can compare and isolate exactly how the incident affected the system.
A SOC analyst cares because a coherent timeline turns scattered evidence into a clear attack narrative, pinpointing the initial compromise, lateral movement, and impact for reporting and remediation.
timeline analysis.exam: Look for questions distinguishing a super timeline (built with Plaso when the incident time is unknown) from a targeted timeline (used when the incident time is known).

explain: Forensic analysis frequently centers on timeline analysis, the technique of searching through many log files and artifacts to merge their timestamps into a single unified timeline of events.
Timeline analysis utilities such as Plaso automate this correlation, parsing dozens of artifact types and normalizing their timestamps into one dataset.

A super timeline is built when the analyst is not sure when the event occurred and therefore needs every available artifact folded in, whereas a targeted timeline is used when the analyst already has a good idea of when the event occurred and can focus the window.

An analyst cares because choosing the right timeline scope keeps an investigation efficient, avoiding drowning in noise on a super timeline when a focused targeted timeline would answer the question faster.
forensic analysis.exam: Expect questions that test timeline-analysis vocabulary, including the Plaso super timeline for unknown event times and the targeted timeline for known event times.

explain: Packet capture tools record network traffic off the wire or air so analysts can inspect the actual contents of communications during and after an incident.

Wireshark is the leading graphical packet analyzer and tshark is its command-line counterpart, both included in analyst distributions such as Security Onion, and they decode protocols and let investigators filter and follow conversations.

For wireless investigations the Aircrack-ng suite is standard, where airmon-ng places an adapter into monitor mode, airodump-ng captures 802.11 frames and enumerates access points and clients, and Aircrack-ng itself performs key cracking against captured handshakes.
A SOC analyst cares because captured packets provide ground-truth evidence of data exfiltration, command-and-control, and credential theft that logs alone may not reveal.
packet capture tools.exam: Look for questions matching tools to tasks, such as Wireshark or tshark for full packet capture and the Aircrack-ng suite (airmon-ng, airodump-ng) for wireless capture and analysis.

explain: Data privacy and data security are related but distinct concepts, where privacy is about the individual and the appropriate collection and use of their information, and security is about protecting the data itself from unauthorized access.

Privacy also differs from confidentiality, since confidentiality is a security property focused on keeping data secret through controls, while privacy is focused on keeping an individual's identity and personal information governed by how the data may be used.

Data security is enforced through technical and administrative controls, whereas privacy governs data usage, consent, and handling of data types such as personal data and personally identifiable information (PII).

A security analyst cares because a system can be secure yet still violate privacy through improper use of data, so protecting confidentiality is necessary but not sufficient to meet privacy obligations.
data privacy and security.exam: Expect conceptual questions that ask you to distinguish privacy (about the individual and how data is used) from security and confidentiality (about protecting the data itself).

explain: Nontechnical controls are the administrative and policy measures that govern how data is handled, complementing technical safeguards with rules, roles, and agreements.

They include data ownership, which assigns accountability for a data set, data classification, which labels data by sensitivity to drive handling requirements, and data confidentiality reinforced by a nondisclosure agreement (NDA) that legally binds parties to protect information.

Data sovereignty, the idea that data is subject to the laws of the country where it is collected or stored, is a core principle behind the EU's GDPR, which also mandates data minimization (collect only what is needed) and data purpose limitation (use data only for the stated purpose).
A security analyst cares because these controls define the compliance boundaries the technical program must enforce, and violations expose the organization to regulatory fines and legal liability.
nontechnical controls.exam: Look for questions on data governance terms such as data classification, data ownership, NDAs, data sovereignty as the principle behind GDPR, and data minimization and purpose limitation.
